activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Arya went to the library with her dad. She wanted to make a picture there. The craft table had paper and crayons.

Arya picked a paper. "This is a square," she said. It had four sides that matched. Dad nodded. "A square for you," he said.

The boy next to her had a napkin. He folded it in half, edge to edge. He opened his hands. "Look!" he said. It was not a square now. It was long and flat. Arya tilted her head. "It's a rectangle," said the boy.

Arya tried it too. She lined up the edges. She folded her square paper in half. She pressed it flat. Then she held it up. Her square was a rectangle now! "I did it!" she said.

Dad smiled. "Can you spin your rectangle?" he asked. Arya spun it round and round on the table. The boy clapped.

Then Arya looked at the wall. There was a clock like a circle. There was a flag like a triangle. There was a book like a rectangle, with sharp corners.

"I can make shapes," Arya said. She folded her paper again. She held it up to the window. "Look, Dad. A little rectangle."

Dad gave her a spring clip to hang it up. Arya clipped her paper to the shelf. It flapped a little in the air. "My shape stays here," she said. "For everyone to see."

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story: Olivier was at Grandma's house. His little blue car was lost. "Where can it be?" he asked. Grandma said, "Let's look." Olivier looked under the table. No car. He looked in the toy box. No car. He looked by the big chair. No car. Then Olivier saw something. The cat was asleep. The cat's tail was moving. It tapped a basket. Something inside went bump, bump. Olivier peeked in the basket. "My car!" he said. "It fell in here!" After that, Olivier did a new thing. He put the car in the basket every night. Same basket, by his bed. One morning he wanted his car. He looked in the basket. There it was! "Grandma, I found it so fast!" he called. Grandma smiled. "That naughty cat can't hide it now," Olivier said, and drove the car along the floor.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Max put on his little blue apron. Today he would make pancakes for his family. His tummy was hungry and rumbling.

Teacher Lily held up a card. "This is a recipe," she said. "It tells us what to use and what to do, one step at a time." Max wanted to pour, pour, pour. He mixed the flour. He cracked the egg. Then he skipped ahead. He forgot to add the milk!

Teacher Lily poured the batter on the pan. Max watched. The pancakes did not puff up. They sat flat, flat, flat like little pillows that got squashed. "Oh no," said Max. "Flat pancakes!"

"Let's read the recipe again," said Teacher Lily. They looked at the card together. One step, two steps, three steps. "There," said Max. He pointed at the milk. "I missed the milk!"

They mixed a new bowl. Flour, egg, and milk too. This time the pancakes puffed up big and round. Max counted them. One, two, three, four. He carried them to the family table all by himself.

"Yum," said Daddy, taking a big bite. Max giggled and said, "One more step? Butter!"

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Joshua went to the park with Mom. He brought his blue ball. But when it was time to play, the ball was gone. Joshua looked under the bench. He looked by the slide. No ball. Joshua felt like crying. "It is hard to lose your ball," said Mom. "Let's look some more."

They walked past the swings. They saw the park helper, Mr. Lee. Mr. Lee held a blue ball. "Is this yours?" he asked. "There is a name tag on it. It says Joshua." Mom had written Joshua's name on the tag at home. Mr. Lee read the name. Then he gave the ball back to Joshua.

Joshua hugged his ball. "Thank you, Mr. Lee!" he said. "Do you want to share it with me?" asked Mr. Lee. Joshua rolled the ball to him. Mr. Lee rolled it back. They played and played. Joshua smiled and held his name tag tight. "My name," he said. "That is me!"

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Arthur rode the bus with his mom. Snow was starting to fall outside. Arthur held his hands in his lap. His bunny was not there. Bunny was lost at Grandma's house.

"Where could bunny be?" Arthur wondered. The bus stopped. Grandma was waiting. Arthur ran inside. He zoomed from room to room. He peeked fast in the kitchen. He peeked fast in the bedroom. No bunny anywhere!

Arthur sat down on the rug. Some dirt from his shoe sat there too. He took a big breath. "I will look in one room at a time," he said. He looked all around the kitchen. He looked under the table. No bunny. Then he looked all around the bedroom. He looked under the bed. There was bunny's neat little ear! Arthur pulled bunny out and hugged him tight. "I found you," he whispered.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Alexander wanted Grandpa to read the owl book. It had a big brown owl on the cover. "Please read it now," said Alexander.

Grandpa sat down on the couch. He picked up the book. He squinted at the page. Then he reached for his glasses. He put them on his nose. "Now I can see the words," said Grandpa. "Glasses help me see more clearly."

Alexander wanted to try. "Can I see with them?" he asked. "Just for a minute," said Grandpa. Alexander put on the big glasses. Everything looked funny and blurry. The room looked too big. He took them off fast. His eyes saw clearly again without the glasses. "How curious," said Alexander. "They help you. But not me!"

Then Grandpa began to read. Alexander heard the story with his ears. He smelled popcorn from the kitchen. Mom brought warm popcorn in a bowl. Alexander touched the bumpy kernels with his fingers. He tasted one. It was salty and good.

"Was that owl real?" Alexander asked at the end. "No, but there was one at the zoo," said Grandpa. "Can we go see it?" asked Alexander. Grandpa laughed and put his glasses back on.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Ibrahim woke up. The sun was up too. Mama smiled at him. "Time to brush your teeth," she said. "We brush in the morning." Ibrahim brushed. One, two, three, up and down. His teeth felt good.

At breakfast, Ibrahim ate his egg. Then he played. Then Papa ran the bath. Papa made the water warm with his own hand. Ibrahim got in and splashed. He got dressed all by himself. His sock had a little rip in it. "New socks tomorrow," said Mama.

Night came. The lamp was off. Ibrahim was in bed. Then he sat up. "Mama! My teeth!" He hopped out of bed. He ran to the sink. He brushed and brushed. "We brush before bed too," said Mama. "Good boy, Ibrahim." She tucked him in. She kissed his head. "One kiss," she said. "Two kisses." Ibrahim smiled and closed his eyes.

story:
Edouard ran into the playroom. He had five toy monkeys in his hands. "Let's sing!" he said. He lined them up on the bed toy. Then he began to sing. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!"

He pushed one monkey. Bonk! It fell off the bed. Edouard laughed. Now there were four monkeys left. He sang again. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed!" One more fell off. Bonk! Now there were three.

He turned the last monkeys around to face him. He sang and sang. One fell, then one more. At last, one monkey sat alone on the bed. "One little monkey jumping on the bed!" Bonk! It fell off too. Edouard looked. No monkeys on the bed. He picked up all ten of his hands' worth, one, two, three, four, five. "Again!" he shouted, and lined them back up.

story:
Eliana and her brother Sam played trains. The trains were loud. They went click clack on the track. Then Sam grabbed the blue train. Eliana grabbed it too. "My turn," said Eliana. Sam let go. Then he got the next turn. That felt fair.

Eliana wished she could keep the blue train all day. But she gave it back. "Your turn," she said. Sam smiled big.

Then it was time for snack. Eliana ran to the kitchen. The toy room stayed messy. Mama was there cutting apples with a safe knife. Eliana watched from her stool.

"Eliana, your trains are still out," said Mama. "Everyone helps clean up the toys they played with." Eliana ran back. She picked up the trains. They felt hard and smooth in her hands. Sam picked up his blocks. Under one block was a red pencil! "Look!" said Eliana. She put it in the cup.

The room was clean. Then they ate sweet apple slices together.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Nathan stood by the little pool at the lake. His teacher was not there yet. The water was blue and cool. Nathan could hear it splash, splash on the side.

A big cow stood in the lake nearby. The cow liked to bathe in the cool water. "Look at the cow," said Nathan's dad. Dad held Nathan's hand. "I want to jump in now," said Nathan. He stepped toward the pool. "Not yet," said Dad kindly. "A grown-up must always watch children when they are in or near water." Nathan stopped and sat down. He put his toes near the edge and waited.

Soon the teacher came. She smiled and said, "I am watching now, Nathan." Then Nathan jumped in. He kicked his legs. The water made little waves. His dad clapped. Nathan felt happy. "I did it," he said, splashing with his hands.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Oliver sat at the kitchen table. Mom put down two rows of buttons. One row was long and spread out. One row was bunched up close. "That one has more!" said Oliver. He pointed at the long row. "I want the row with more!"

"Count them," said Mom. Oliver touched each button in the long row. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted the bunched-up row. "One, two, three, four, five." He sat very still. Both rows had five!

Oliver pushed the close buttons apart. They made a long row too. He counted again. "Still five!" He pushed them back together. He counted again. "Five!" He laughed out loud. "Moving them doesn't change it!"

A bee bumped at the window. Oliver ran to look. "Come back!" he cried. He waved his soft sleeve at the glass. Then he ran back to the table. He spread the buttons out one more time. "Five, five, five!"

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Emmett sat at the kitchen table. Mom put down three warm bowls of soup. Grandma put down one orange cup. Emmett had his own little spoon.

Grandma smiled at everyone. "Bon appétit," she said. Emmett looked up. "What does that mean?" he asked. "It is what people say in France," said Grandma. "We say it before we eat. It means, have a good meal." Grandma had lived in France when she was young.

Emmett wanted to say it too. He tried. "Bone apple tea," he said. Grandma laughed softly. "Almost," she said. "Bon appétit." Emmett listened. He held his spoon like a pencil, very still. "Bon appétit," he said. Mom clapped. "Perfect!"

Dad came in with bread. Emmett sat up tall. "Bon appétit, Dad," he said. Dad grinned big. "Bon appétit to you, Emmett."

Grandma took a sip of soup. "One bowl, two bowls, three bowls," she said. "And one happy little boy at our table." Emmett dipped his spoon. "Bon appétit," he whispered to his soup.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Zachary sat on the big rug in the living room. The tablet lay on the coffee table. He wanted to draw a red truck on it.

He pressed the little round button. The screen lit up. He tapped the blue square, and the drawing app opened. A white page waited for him. Zachary drew two round wheels. He drew a long red body. He drew a fast truck going down a hill.

Then the screen went black. All his truck was gone. "Oh no," said Zachary. "Where did my truck go? Did I forget to tap something?"

Dad came over and looked. "The tablet ran out of power," he said. "It needs charging now."

Dad plugged the charger into the wall and into the tablet. A small green line showed up on the screen. Zachary watched it. "Is it getting juice?" he asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Power for the tablet."

They set the tablet on the shelf to charge. Zachary put his crayons away too. Later the screen woke up. Zachary opened the app, and there was his red truck. He drew a sun above it. "Hi, truck," he said.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Mila was going on a trip. Her family was going to a campsite with a tent. She put her teddy bear in her little red backpack.

First they had to ride on a big plane. At the airport, Mila saw a long desk. A kind man in a uniform stood there.

Mila put her backpack on a moving belt. The backpack went into a big machine. The machine checks what is inside bags. Then the backpack was gone.

"My teddy!" said Mila. "Where is my teddy?"

Dad held her hand. "Watch the belt," he said.

Mila watched. She watched and watched. Then the backpack came out the other end of the machine. It slid down to her.

Mila opened the bag. Her teddy was still there. She hugged him tight.

"My teddy came out," she said. "The machine gave him back!"

A lady at the desk smiled at Mila. Mila stood tall and proud. She held her teddy all the way to the plane.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Joshua wanted to make a growly bear sound. Miss Amy said, "Try the big piano." Joshua sat near the piano. He pressed a key on the right side. The sound was high, like a little bird. "That is not a bear," said Joshua. He tried the right side again. High, high, high. Still a little bird.

Miss Amy smiled. "Try the other side," she said. Joshua pressed a key on the left side. Boom! A big, low sound came out. "Growl!" said Joshua. He pressed more keys on the left. Low sounds rumbled out. Low, low, low. A car went by outside, and it sounded low too.

Joshua made his bear growl and growl. Then he played the right side again, just to hear the little bird. "Growl," he said. "Tweet," he said. Miss Amy laughed. Joshua played one low key and one high key, over and over, until it was time to stop. "Same time tomorrow?" asked Miss Amy. "Yes," said Joshua. He waved to the piano. "Bye, bear."

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Charles rode the big city bus. He held his sleepy bear. The bus went bump. The bear flew out of his hands. "Oh no!" said Charles. "My bear!"

Charles looked down. The bear was gone. It was dark under the seat. Charles could not see anything under there. He got on his knees and peeked. It was just black and shadowy.

The bus driver saw him. She reached up and clicked a little light on her keys. "Here is a flashlight," she said. "A flashlight helps you see into dark spots, like under a bed." She gave it to Mom. Mom held it and shined it under the seat.

The light made the dark spot bright. There was the bear! His arm was stuck on a string that hung down. Mom pulled the string aside. Charles reached in and grabbed the bear. He hugged him tight. The bear felt warm and soft. "Thank you," Charles said to the driver. The driver smiled. Charles sat on Mom's lap. He patted the bear's head. "Sleepy time, bear," he said.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Nova sat at the craft table at summer camp. She was drawing a big red apple. One leaf, two leaves, three leaves. She wanted the leaves very, very dark green.

Nova pressed down hard. She pressed harder. Then she pressed her hardest. Snap! The pencil point broke off and flew onto the table.

"Oh no," said Nova. "My point went pop!"

The camp teacher, Sam, came over. "That pencil needs a new point," he said. He sharpened it with his sharpener, slowly and safely.

Nova picked up her pencil again. This time she pressed gently, like a little cat walking. One leaf, two leaves, three leaves. All soft green, all whole.

"My pencil is still alive," said Nova.

Sam laughed. "It likes you better now," he said.

Nova drew a little toy bear next to the apple. She even drew her old red hat. Then she held up her picture.

"Look, everybody!" she said. "One apple, one bear, one hat, and one happy pencil."

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Sofia went to the bank with Mama. Sofia carried her own little bag of coins. She put the coins on the counter, one by one. The coins made a small fall into the tray. Ping, ping, ping.

Then it was time to go. Outside the big doors, snowflakes began to float down. Sofia put on her coat by herself. She pulled the zipper tab up, up, up. But the zipper would not close. She pulled again. Still nothing.

"Mama, my zipper is stuck," Sofia said.

Mama did not pull the tab. She held the coat and looked. "See the little box at the bottom?" she said.

Sofia looked down. Yes! There was a tiny box at the bottom of one side. And the other side had a little end. Sofia slid the end into the box. It clicked in. Then she pulled the tab. Zip! The coat closed all the way.

Sofia zipped it down and up again. Zip, zip. Now the wind could not get in.

"Ready?" Mama asked.

Sofia pushed the door open. The snowflakes floated past her warm, zipped-up coat.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Luca stood at the farm with his papa. He had three little seeds in his hand. One seed, two seeds, three seeds. Papa dug a row in the dirt. Luca dropped the seeds in. Papa covered them with soft brown soil.

"Will my seeds grow today?" Luca asked. "No, they need many days," said Papa. So Luca watered the dirt with his small blue can. Then he waited.

Each morning Luca ran to the garden. He saw dirt. He saw dirt. He saw more dirt. A naughty crow flew by, but the seeds stayed hidden and safe. Luca kept on watering. One day, two days, many days.

Then Luca saw something new. Something small and green stood up out of the soil. "Papa, come quick!" he called. Papa came fast. "What is it?" Luca asked. "A tiny new plant poking up out of the soil is called a sprout," said Papa. "A sprout," said Luca. He smiled at the little green sprout. He took a picture of it with Mama's camera, click.

The next day there were two sprouts. Then three sprouts, one for each seed. Luca watered them again. "Grow big, sprouts," he said. "I will fish in the pond while you grow." He sat by the water with Papa, and the sprouts waved in the soft wind.

story:
Amira sat at the big table in math club. She had a little bucket of blocks. "Let's count them," said her friend Tom. Amira touched each block. "One, two, three, four," she said. She had four blocks. Tom had a big pile too. "Who has more?" asked Teacher Nan. Amira looked at both piles. Tom's pile looked big. "Tom has more," she said. She counted his blocks. "One, two, three, four, five." Tom had five. He had more than four.

Then Grandma came in. She had something in her hand. "This one is for you," Grandma said. It was a shiny red block. Amira put it in her bucket. She hoped it would help. She counted again. "One, two, three, four, five." Now she had five too! "Look, look," said Amira. "I got one more. Now I have five!" Tom put one of his blocks in her bucket too. Amira counted. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Now she had six!

"Who has more now?" asked Teacher Nan. Tom counted his blocks. He had four. "Amira has more," said Tom. Amira smiled and hugged her bucket. "Ready for more blocks," she said. Grandma laughed and dropped one more block in. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven," counted Amira.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Rowan ran to the playground in his blue shirt. The sun felt warm on his face. He heard a kite humming in the wind. It was red, with a long tail. One, two, three ribbons on the tail.

A girl named Mia held the string. Rowan wanted the kite so much. He reached out his hand. Mia pulled the string away. Her face looked scared. Rowan stopped. His tummy felt small and tight.

Then he remembered Grandpa's words. "Say 'May I have a turn?'" Grandpa had said. "It is the polite way to ask." Rowan took a big breath. "May I have a turn?" he asked. Mia smiled. "Yes! Hold tight like this." She put the string in his hand. The kite pulled and pulled. It tickled his fingers. "Thank you," said Rowan. "You can kick off your shoes if you want," said Mia.

A big boy ran past and bumped Rowan's arm. "Sorry," the big boy said. He helped Rowan hold the string again. One, two, three ribbons danced in the sky. "May I have a turn next?" Mia asked. Rowan laughed and gave her the string.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Mohamed sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump, down the road. "Mama, where are we going?" he asked. "To Grandma's house," said Mama. "She will make pancakes." Mohamed loved pancakes. It was his dream to eat a big stack of them. He looked out the window. He saw a red car and an empty truck. "Mama, does Grandma cook pancakes on the stove?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. "The stove gets hot." Mohamed thought about that. "Is it hot when it looks cold?" he asked. "Yes," said Mama. "A stove can be hot even when it does not look hot."

Soon the car stopped. Mohamed held Mama's hand in the parking lot. He stayed close to her, just like a little duck stays close to its mama. At Grandma's house, the kitchen smelled sweet. Grandma stirred the batter. "Is the stove hot now?" Mohamed asked Grandma. "It is hot, but only I touch it," said Grandma. Mohamed kept his hands in his lap. He watched a pancake bubble. He heard it sizzle. Grandma flipped it high in the air. "Wow!" said Mohamed. They sat down to talk and eat. Mohamed took a big bite. "Grandma, the pancake is warm and yummy!" he said. Grandma smiled and poured more batter into the pan.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Weston sat at the dinner table. His plate had yummy noodles. He ate them all up. Now his tummy still wanted more.

The doorbell rang. Ding dong!

Weston slid under the table and hid. It was Mr. Bean from next door. His boots went tap, tap on the floor.

Mom said, "Weston, Mr. Bean is here."

Weston peeked out from under the tablecloth. Mr. Bean waved his big hand.

Weston climbed into his chair. He took a big breath. "Hello, Mr. Bean," he said.

Mr. Bean's face turned into a big smile. "Hello, Weston!" he said. "I heard a little storm under that table."

Weston giggled. "The storm went away," he said.

Then Weston held out his plate. "More noodles, please, Mom."

Mom filled his plate. "Here you go," she said.

"Thank you," said Weston.

Mr. Bean sat down too. Mom gave him a bowl. Weston showed him how to twirl noodles with a fork. Mr. Bean made a wobbly nest.

Weston laughed so hard his toes tickled.

One noodle slipped off Weston's fork. It landed on Mr. Bean's shoe.

"Sorry," said Weston.

"That's okay," said Mr. Bean. He picked it up with a napkin.

After dinner, Mr. Bean stood up. "Time to go home," he said. "Goodbye, Weston."

"Bye bye," said Weston. He waved his whole hand, just like Mr. Bean had waved his.

When it was time to go home, Dad said, "Now we put it away." He helped her tap the button. The screen went dark. Iris patted the tablet, soft and gentle. "Bye, monkey," she said. "See you next time."

story:
Kinsley wanted her red nightlight. It made stars on the ceiling. But the nightlight was not plugged in.

She looked behind the couch. There was a small hole in the wall. It had little slots in it. "An outlet," Mama called it. The nightlight plug went there. Kinsley knew just what to do. She ran to the kitchen. "Mama, I found the outlet!" she said.

Mama put down her cup. Steam rose from the cup. "That steam is hot," Mama said. "Only grown-ups touch hot things." She held Kinsley's hand. They walked to the couch together. Mama pushed the plug in. The nightlight glowed. Stars spread across the ceiling. "My stars came back," said Kinsley.

Outside, soft snow fell on the window. Kinsley sat close to Mama on the couch. She had painted a picture that day. It was a picture of stars. Now the real stars shined beside her paint. "Stay close," said Mama. Kinsley leaned in. The little stars danced above them both.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Wesley wanted to play a guessing game. He got a cup, a toothbrush, and a towel. He put them in a basket.

"I will guess with my eyes closed," Wesley said. He closed his eyes tight. He did not peek.

Daddy held out the first thing. Wesley touched it with his fingertips. His fingertips said the cup was smooth and cool. "The cup!" he said. He was right.

Next his fingertips felt the toothbrush. It was bumpy on top. The handle was smooth. "The toothbrush!" he said. Right again.

Then the towel. His fingertips said it was soft and fluffy. "The towel!" Wesley laughed.

Wesley heard the water drip in the sink. He smelled the soap, so sweet. Daddy gave him a tiny taste of toothpaste on his finger. It tasted minty, and Wesley made a funny face.

"My fingertips can tell if something is soft, rough, smooth or bumpy," Wesley said.

"You guessed every one," said Daddy.

Wesley held the cup up straight. "My turn to pick for you, Daddy. Close your eyes!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Paisley wanted a bedtime story. She ran to get her book. She climbed into bed with it.

She opened the book and looked at the page. The words looked all mixed up. The pictures seemed backwards too. "That's funny," she said. The story did not make sense this way.

Paisley turned the book over. Now she saw the front cover. It had a bear on it. She opened the front cover and turned the first page. The words sat in neat little rows. The pictures came in order. The bear found honey, then took a nap.

Papa came in and sat down. "Read it to me," Paisley said. Papa started at the front and turned page after page. Paisley listened and played with her blanket corner.

The last page came. Papa closed the back cover. "The end," he said.

"Again," said Paisley. Papa opened the front cover one more time.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Zayn put on his red shoe. "We need to go to the library," said Mama. "You get your very own card today."

At the library, a lady smiled. She made a card with Zayn's name on it. "My card!" said Zayn. He held it tight. He picked a book about a big, juicy strawberry. The lady scanned his card. Zayn took the book home.

The next week, Zayn gave the book back. "Now what?" he asked. He looked at his card. Was it all done? He gave the card to the lady. She scanned it again. "Pick a new book," she said. Zayn gasped. The same card worked again! He ran to the shelf. He chose a book about a sleepy moon.

"Home, moon book," said Zayn. He hugged his card all the way.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Miles ran into the pool changing room. He put his towel in the cubby. His swimming bag had a big owl on it.

"Time to swim!" said Dad.

Miles got in the pool. He kicked and splashed. He practiced and practiced. "Look at me!" he said.

Then it was time to get out. Miles grabbed the side of the pool. He pulled and pulled. His arms slipped. He fell back with a splash.

"Sorry, I can't do it," said Miles.

"Where are the steps?" Dad asked.

"The steps?" said Miles. "Can steps help?"

"Try them and see," said Dad.

Miles swam to the pool steps. He climbed up, up, up. One step. Two steps. Out!

"Easy peasy," said Miles. Then he hopped down and climbed out again.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
David climbed the tall steps of the school bus. It was his first day of school. He found a seat by the window. The bus went bump, bump, bump.

At school, everyone went inside. David saw blocks and paints and a big rug. He wanted to play with everything. Then his tummy felt funny. He needed to find the bathroom. Where was it? He looked left. He looked right. He did not see it.

A tall lady walked over. "I am Miss Kim," she said. "I am the teacher." David took a big breath. "Where is the bathroom?" he asked. Miss Kim smiled. "It is right over there," she said. She pointed to a small door. "If you need help at school, you can ask the teacher."

David walked to the door. He pushed it open. He found the bathroom all by himself, well, almost by himself. When he came back, he asked, "Can you teach me the blocks?" "Yes!" said Miss Kim. David built a tall, tall tower. It went up and up and up. Then it fell down with a crash. David laughed and built it again.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Everett sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted to feel brave, like a big boy.

The doctor came in. She was a kind man's helper with white shoes. "Everett, can you see my light?" she asked. Everett used his eyes to see it blink. Then she rang a little bell. Everett used his ears to hear it ring. "Good listening," she said.

Next she held out a cotton ball. Everett sniffed it with his nose. "Smells like nothing," he said. Then the doctor put a small wet cloth on his arm. Everett touched it with his fingers. "Cold," he said. "That's your skin doing its job," the doctor said.

Then the doctor gave Everett a lemon slice. Everett thought it would taste sweet, like his orange juice at home. He took a little lick with his tongue. His whole face scrunched up. "Sour," he said. "Sour, sour, sour!" The doctor laughed. "Your tongue can taste that a lemon is sour." Everett tried again, a tiny lick. Still sour. He climbed down from the big chair all by himself.

"I used my eyes and my ears and my nose," said Everett. "And my fingers and my tongue too." He gave the doctor a high five. "Same time next year," she said. Everett waved all the way to the door.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Madelyn sat at the table. She wanted juice. "Give me juice!" she said.

Grandpa shook his head. "Try again," he said. Madelyn thought. Then she said, "Juice, please."

Grandpa smiled. "Here you go," he said. He poured the juice. Madelyn drank it. It was cold and sweet.

"Thank you," said Madelyn. Grandpa patted her head. Madelyn felt big.

Then Madelyn ran to the door. The dog was outside. The dog began to bark. A butterfly flew by the window. "Help, Grandpa!" said Madelyn. "I want to see the butterfly!"

Grandpa opened the door. They watched together. The butterfly flew up, up, up. Then it was gone.

Madelyn ran back inside. She bumped the table. Her cup fell. Juice went everywhere.

"Sorry, Grandpa," said Madelyn.

"That is okay," said Grandpa. He wiped the floor. Madelyn helped with her little towel. Soon the floor was clean.

Madelyn yawned. Her eyes closed. She fell asleep in her chair. Grandpa carried her to bed. "Goodnight, Madelyn," he said. The dog barked one soft bark.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Mia ran into the baby store. She held Mama's hand tight. "The baby comes soon!" said Mia. It was windy outside. The door swung shut behind them.

Mia saw cribs. She saw tiny socks. She saw a big shelf of dolls. "Can I pick one?" asked Mia. "Yes," said Mama. Mia chose a doll with a soft round head. Then she saw it. The doll's head tipped way back. It flopped like a sleepy flower.

"Uh oh," said Mia. She put her small hand under the doll's head. The head stayed up. "Look, Mama! I fixed it!" Mama smiled. "A new baby can't hold up his head," said Mama. "So we hold it for him." Mia carried the doll through the whole store. Her hand stayed under the head the whole way.

At home, snow started to fall. Big white flakes came down. Mia had an idea. She put the doll in the new little crib. She tucked a soft blanket around it. Then she tapped the doll's head, very gently. The head rolled to one side. So Mia reached in and cupped it with her hand.

Daddy called from the car. "Time to get Mama! The baby is coming today!" Mia picked up her doll. One hand under the bottom. One hand behind the head. She marched to the door. "I'm ready, baby brother," said Mia. "I will hold your head."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Victoria was home with a cold. Her nose was runny. She sniffed and sniffed at breakfast. One sniff. Two sniffs. Three sniffs.

Mom put down her cup. "You need a tissue, honey." Victoria took one. She blew her little nose. The tissue felt soft. The runny nose felt better.

"Thank you," said Victoria. "My nose was all stuffy before." Mom gave her a hug.

Later, Victoria looked out the window. The sky was cloudy. She saw the big tree sway in the wind. She hoped she could play under the tree soon.

Her nose ran again. Victoria sniffed once. Then she knew just what to do. "Mom, tissue please!" Mom brought the box.

"One tissue for Victoria," said Mom. "Two tissues." Victoria giggled. She put the tissues in the bin all by herself.

"Do you want some warm soup later?" Mom asked.

Victoria nodded. "Yes please. With a spoon."

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Edouard sat in the music room at school. Miss Lily played a song on the piano. Everyone had to clap along.

Edouard clapped too fast. Then he clapped too slow. "Why can't I do it?" he asked. Miss Lily smiled. "Try clapping when I nod," she said.

Edouard watched her head. Nod, clap. Nod, clap. Soon his hands went with the beat. The drum in the corner boomed, and his claps fit right in. "It works!" he shouted. Tom laughed and clapped too.

"Can we sing a long song now?" Edouard asked. Miss Lily shook her head. "No, a nursery rhyme," she said. "A nursery rhyme is a short rhyming song for little ones."

So they sang "Twinkle, Twinkle." Edouard clapped and sang. He did not forget one single word. His brother at home would hear it tonight.

At pick-up time, Edouard sang it to his brother. "Again!" his brother said.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Alexander went to the baby store with Mom. He wanted to pick a toy. He found a soft red ball. "The baby can spin it with me!" he said.

At home, the baby was sleeping. Again. Alexander waited and waited. He watched the baby's small face. "Does the baby sleep all day?" he asked. Mom said, "New babies sleep for much of the day." Alexander set the red ball by the crib.

The baby woke up for a little while. Alexander held out the ball. The baby grabbed it with tiny fingers. Then the baby's eyes closed. Baby was sleeping again. Alexander got his cup and sat close by. "I will wait right here," he said. The soft red ball waited too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Ava sat at the art table. She wanted to draw a house. But her windows looked lost and wobbly. "My windows won't come out right," she said.

Miss Kim came to help. She took a toy block from the shelf. "Put a sticker on each face," she said. Ava pressed a red sticker on one face. Then another. One, two, three, four, five, six. Six stickers on six faces. Each face was a square, just like her window!

Ava traced a face with her finger. The block felt cool on her skin. Then she traced around the block on her paper. A square came out! "A square window!" she said.

She drew more shapes too. A circle sun. A triangle roof. A rectangle door. Squares one by one, all in a row.

Miss Kim hung the picture on the wall. Ava counted her windows out loud. "One, two, three, four, five, six."

Miss Kim clapped her hands.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Madison ran onto the basketball court. The sun was warm on her arms. The weather was hot and dry. Her team wore blue shirts today.

Coach Maya blew her whistle. "Break time!" she called. All the players ran to the bench. They picked up their water bottles and drank. Madison looked for her bottle. It was not there. She had left it at home.

"Where is my water?" Madison asked. "Can I play without it?"

Coach Maya shook her head gently. "Not on a hot day like this," she said. "Players drink water during breaks." She brought a cool bottle over from her big bag. The bottle felt smooth and cold in Madison's hands. She took big sips. The water was wet and sweet.

Madison went back to the game. She bounced the ball. She aimed at the hoop. The ball went in! Her whole team clapped.

Madison smiled. Next time, she would remember her bottle. "Coach, may I put it in your bag?" she asked.

"Yes," said Coach Maya. "Good thinking, Madison."

Madison dropped the ball into Coach Maya's bag and ran back to the hoop.
